headline: Keysight: revenue up 41% and orders up 53% on AI networking demand, yet the shares fall 7% after a record year
takeaway: Fourth-quarter revenue rose 41% to $1.99 billion and non-GAAP EPS nearly doubled to $3.61, beating the $3.38 consensus. Orders of $2.34 billion ran well ahead of revenue and first-quarter guidance points to further growth, but the shares fell 7% the next day as investors took profits after a strong run.
results: Keysight Technologies reported revenue of $1.99 billion for the quarter ended October 31, up 41% from $1.42 billion, and orders of $2.34 billion, up 53%. GAAP net income doubled to $486 million, or $2.82 a share; non-GAAP EPS was $3.61 against $1.91 a year earlier. Operating cash flow was $507 million and free cash flow $465 million, and the company ended the year with $2.92 billion of cash.

The Communications Solutions Group, which sells test equipment to network, chip and device makers, grew 51% to $1,496 million, with commercial communications up 73% and aerospace, defence and government up 7%. The Electronic Industrial Solutions Group grew 16% to $498 million on semiconductor, automotive and energy demand.

For fiscal 2026 revenue rose 33% to $7.16 billion, orders 49% to $8.13 billion and non-GAAP EPS 64% to $11.72, with free cash flow of $1.75 billion. Keysight spent $669 million buying back stock during the year.
mgmt: Chief executive Satish Dhanasekaran called fiscal 2026 the strongest year in Keysight’s history, with robust order and revenue growth and significant earnings expansion, and said investments to differentiate the portfolio position the company to grow and outperform its markets in fiscal 2027.

For the first quarter of fiscal 2027 Keysight expects revenue of $2.04 billion to $2.06 billion and non-GAAP EPS of $3.63 to $3.69, both above the fourth-quarter level and well ahead of a year earlier.
view: Keysight sells the instruments that engineers use to test whether chips, network equipment and radios work as designed, and the AI build-out has turned it from a steady 5%-growth company into a high-growth one. Data centres built for AI need far faster connections between processors — 800-gigabit and 1.6-terabit optical links, new generations of PCIe and Ethernet — and every new standard requires a new generation of test gear. Commercial communications up 73% is that cycle in a single number, boosted further by the acquisition of Spirent, the network-testing company Keysight bought in 2025.

The order figure is the most encouraging part of the release. Orders of $2.34 billion against revenue of $1.99 billion is a book-to-bill of about 1.17, meaning the backlog is growing and next year’s revenue is partly visible already. The first-quarter guide confirms it. Margins have also expanded sharply: non-GAAP EPS grew far faster than revenue, showing the operating leverage in a business with high fixed research costs.

So why did the shares fall 7%? Partly because the stock had nearly doubled over the year and was priced for perfection at around 30 times trailing earnings, and partly because the first-quarter guide, though strong, implies sequential growth slowing to low single digits. Test-equipment demand is notoriously cyclical: customers buy heavily when a new standard arrives and pause once labs are equipped. The question for 2027 is whether AI networking produces a sustained multi-year cycle, as management argues, or a burst followed by a digestion period. The orders say the cycle is still building.
watch: Watch orders against revenue in the first quarter, the growth rate in commercial communications as 1.6-terabit equipment ramps, and any full-year 2027 framework management offers in February.
